I've been farming our land in Quzhou for over thirty years now. I'm 52, and my husband works off-farm in the county town, so most days it's me making the decisions and doing the field work. We have about 6 mu of good flat land, and I've learned that sticking with what works is better than gambling on something new. Every year I grow winter wheat and summer maize in rotation — that's what our well and soil are suited for, and the buyers come right to the village to collect it. 

Last October I planted improved wheat seed on 5 mu after rotary tilling the field. The wheat is up and green now, and with the weather warming, I need to topdress it soon. The extension agent told us 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I always put down a bit more — around 16 kg — because I'd rather waste a little money on fertilizer than risk a bad harvest. I use compound fertilizer as the base and then spread urea at jointing. I'll irrigate four times total this wheat season, including the winter watering I already did and three more in spring. The wheat should give me about 500 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.

After we harvest the wheat in early June, the window to plant maize is very tight — sometimes less than a week. Everyone in the village now plants hybrid maize directly into the wheat stubble without ploughing. It saves diesel, saves time, and the yield is still good. I'll plant Denghai or Nongda hybrid seed, whatever the dealer has in stock. For the maize, I put down compound fertilizer at planting and maybe one more round if the leaves look yellow. I figure about 14 kg nitrogen per mu, plus some phosphorus and potassium. I'll irrigate twice for the maize if the summer rains are not enough. I spray pesticides two or three times for each crop — when I see aphids or when the neighbors start spraying, because if you wait too long the insects eat everything.

I thought about cotton, but I'm getting older and my daughter is working in Shijiazhuang, so I don't have the extra labor for hand-picking. Wheat and maize are easier to manage with machines, and I can handle them mostly by myself. That's my plan.
